summary: Describes a simple HTTP-based protocol for WebRTC-based ingestion of content into streaming services and CDNs. It updates RFC 8840 and RFC 8842.

eli5.summary: This is a simple way for a camera app to start sending live video to a streaming site using an ordinary web request to say hello.

questions: how to publish webrtc to a streaming server
subtitle: A one-request HTTP handshake that lets encoders and cameras push live WebRTC video into streaming services.

tldr.problem: WebRTC deliberately leaves out a signaling protocol, which has made it hard to use as an ingest method for broadcast and streaming services and CDNs.
tldr.mechanism: A WHIP client sends its SDP offer in an HTTP POST, gets the SDP answer back in a 201 Created response, and then media flows from client to server over ICE, DTLS and SRTP. Later changes use HTTP PATCH and DELETE on the session URL.
tldr.outcome: WHIP gives encoders and media servers a small, standard way to start and stop WebRTC ingest. It is a Proposed Standard and it updates RFC 8840 and RFC 8842.

facts.label: Session setup
facts.value: HTTP POST with application/sdp, answered by 201 Created

facts.label: Session teardown
facts.value: HTTP DELETE to the session URL

today: RFC 9725 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 8840 and RFC 8842.

sections.title: Why WebRTC Needed an Ingest Protocol
sections.content:
WebRTC describes how to negotiate media with the Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer model, but it intentionally does not specify a signaling transport at the application level. The RFC says this gap has been an obstacle to using WebRTC as an ingestion protocol in broadcast and streaming, where an encoder pushes media to a streaming service or Content Delivery Network (CDN).

Existing signaling options did not fit well. SIP and XMPP are not designed for broadcasting and show no sign of adoption there, and the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) does not support the SDP offer/answer model. WHIP (WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol) is the proposed answer: easy to implement, as easy to use as popular IP-based broadcast protocols, compliant with WebRTC, and usable from both web browsers and standalone encoders.
sections.eli5: Video calls on the web know how to send pictures, but nobody agreed on how to knock on the door first. WHIP is a standard knock for live video.

sections.title: Overview and the Cast of Players
sections.content:
WHIP is built around a one-time exchange of an SDP offer and answer using HTTP POST. That exchange sets up an Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) session between the WHIP client (the encoder or media producer) and the media server. Media then flows one way, from client to server. SDP renegotiation is not supported: no m= sections can change after the first exchange, and only ICE information can be updated, using HTTP PATCH.

The RFC names these roles: the WHIP endpoint (the ingest server that receives the first request, reached at the WHIP endpoint URL), the media server (which receives the media), and the WHIP session (the HTTP resource the endpoint allocates for one ingest, reached at the WHIP session URL).
sections.eli5: You hand a note to the front desk, they hand back a note with a room number, and then you walk to the room and start your show.

sections.title: Setting Up and Ending a Session
sections.content:
The client builds an initial SDP offer following JSEP and sends an HTTP POST to the WHIP endpoint URL with content type application/sdp. The endpoint replies 201 Created with content type application/sdp, the SDP answer as the body, and a Location header pointing to the new WHIP session. A wrong content type or a malformed SDP must be rejected with a 4xx error.

Because media is one-way, the client SHOULD use sendonly in its offer (it MAY use sendrecv), and inactive and recvonly MUST NOT be used. The endpoint MUST answer with recvonly.

To end a session the client MUST send an HTTP DELETE to the session URL, which frees the resources and ends the ICE and DTLS sessions. Consent freshness (RFC 7675) is used to detect a non-graceful disconnect. Endpoints MUST support OPTIONS requests for CORS, and a GET on an endpoint or session must return a 2xx response with no content, since these resources have no representation.
sections.eli5: You ask to start, the server says yes and gives you a ticket number. When you are done, you hand the ticket back and everything is cleaned up.

sections.title: ICE Updates: Trickle ICE and Restarts
sections.content:
ICE finds a working network path through NATs. After the first exchange, the client MAY send an HTTP PATCH to the session URL with media type application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag to add candidates (Trickle ICE) or to perform an ICE restart. Support for both is RECOMMENDED. A session that supports only one of them MUST answer unsupported PATCH requests with 422 Unprocessable Content.

Because PATCH requests can arrive out of order, a session that supports ICE restarts MUST generate a strong entity-tag for the ICE session and return it in an ETag header of the 201 response. A missing entity-tag is answered with 428 Precondition Required and a non-matching one with 412 Precondition Failed.

For Trickle ICE, the server gathers all of its candidates before answering, so it cannot add more later. The client buffers its own candidates until it has the session URL, then sends one aggregated PATCH. A successful candidate update returns 204 No Content with no ETag. For an ICE restart, the client sends new ice-ufrag and ice-pwd values with If-Match: *, and a successful restart returns 200 OK with the new credentials and a new ETag. If a restart fails, the existing ICE session is kept.
sections.eli5: If your Wi-Fi changes while you are streaming, you can quietly tell the server your new route without starting over.

sections.title: WebRTC Constraints
sections.content:
To keep clients and servers simple, WHIP narrows what WebRTC may do. Both sides SHALL support BUNDLE and use the max-bundle policy, with RTP/RTCP multiplexing and the rtcp-mux-only attribute in each bundled m= section.

Only a single MediaStream is supported, so all m= sections carry the same msid, with at least one track and no two tracks of the same media kind. If the endpoint cannot accept the number of streams or tracks, it MUST reject the POST with 422 Unprocessable Content or 400 Bad Request. The RFC notes that future revisions could relax this.

The endpoint SHOULD NOT reject individual m= sections; it should reject the whole request so there are no partially successful ingest sessions. The client SHOULD offer setup:actpass but MAY use active if it implements only the DTLS client role. The client MUST implement full ICE, while a media server with a publicly reachable address MAY support only ICE lite.
sections.eli5: WHIP sets a few house rules, like one show at a time and one camera and one microphone, so that every player and every server can keep up.

sections.title: Redirects, ICE Servers and Extensions
sections.content:
Endpoints and media servers may be on different machines, so load balancing is expected. Clients SHALL support HTTP redirections, and 301 and 302 MUST NOT be used so a POST is not turned into a GET. The preferred status is 307 Temporary Redirect. An overloaded endpoint MAY return 503 Service Unavailable, possibly with Retry-After.

The endpoint MAY give the client STUN/TURN server details in the 201 response as Link headers with rel="ice-server", carrying username and credential attributes. For clients that cannot change servers after creating an offer, the endpoint MAY also return them for an OPTIONS request, though clients are told not to rely on that.

Simulcast (RFC 8853) MAY be negotiated in the SDP. Extensions are announced by the session in the 201 response, one Link header per extension, using a rel value that starts with urn:ietf:params:whip:ext. Clients MUST ignore unknown values and sessions MUST NOT require any extension.
sections.eli5: The front desk might send you to a different room, hand you a map to find your way through the building, or mention optional extras you are free to ignore.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
All WHIP endpoints, sessions and clients MUST support HTTP authentication, and for interoperability they MUST all support bearer token authentication as in RFC 6750. A client configured with a token sends it in the Authorization header on every request to the endpoint or session, except CORS preflight OPTIONS requests. A client with no token MUST NOT send that header.

What the token is and how it is handed out is outside the scope. The RFC suggests JSON Web Tokens or a shared secret in a database, typically given to the user together with the endpoint URL, much like RTMP URLs and stream keys. Servers could instead put an authentication token inside the URLs.
sections.eli5: A bearer token is like a wristband at a concert: show it every time and the staff let you through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
WHIP sits on top of HTTP and WebRTC, so their security considerations apply, and HTTPS SHALL be used to preserve the WebRTC security model. The RFC adds three attack surfaces specific to the REST methods.

  • POST flooding: an attacker with valid credentials can force the endpoint to allocate resources for many sessions that never connect. Endpoints SHOULD rate limit initial POSTs.
  • Guessable session URLs: if session URLs are easy to guess, an attacker could DELETE running sessions. Endpoints SHOULD generate URLs with enough randomness from a cryptographically secure generator and rate limit DELETE requests.
  • PATCH flooding: repeated PATCH requests can also exhaust resources, so endpoints SHOULD rate limit them too.
sections.eli5: Keep the doors locked, make ticket numbers hard to guess, and do not let one person ring the doorbell a million times.

items.desc: Sent to the WHIP endpoint with an application/sdp offer; answered by 201 Created and a Location header.

items.label: Update ICE

items.label: End a session
items.desc: Sent to the session URL; frees resources and ends the ICE and DTLS sessions.

items.desc: Must be supported by endpoints for CORS; may also return STUN/TURN configuration.

items.label: No content
items.desc: Endpoints and sessions must return a 2xx response with no content.
